opus-5.5.text:
For me, LLM infrastructure is everything between the model weights and the user getting a useful response. That covers the inference engine, scheduling and batching, memory management for things like the KV cache, distributed serving across many GPUs, and increasingly the systems that support training and reinforcement learning loops. It's the layer that decides whether a model is fast, affordable, and reliable in practice, or just impressive on paper.

What we want to build at RadixArk grows out of what we learned working on SGLang. The workloads have changed a lot. A few years ago most people thought of inference as one prompt in, one completion out. Now you have agents making dozens of calls, long multi-turn contexts, structured outputs, tool use, and RL rollouts generating huge volumes of samples. These workloads share a lot of structure, such as common prefixes and repeated context. If the infrastructure understands that structure, through ideas like RadixAttention and prefix caching, you can get large gains in throughput and cost without changing the model at all.

So the infrastructure we want to build has three main properties.

First, it should be **performant by design**. It should co-design the runtime with how people actually program LLMs, rather than treating every request as independent.

Second, it should be **open and general**. It should run well across different models, different hardware vendors, and different scales, from a single GPU up to large clusters. We think a strong open-source foundation is healthier for the whole ecosystem than everyone rebuilding their own closed stack.

Third, it should be **production-grade**. Research systems often show a great benchmark number, but companies need stability, observability, and easy deployment. A big part of RadixArk's mission is closing that gap, so frontier techniques from the open-source community become something any team can depend on.

In one sentence: we want to be the infrastructure layer that makes serving and training large models efficient and accessible for everyone, not only for the handful of labs that can afford to build it all in-house.

r001.rationale: The response mentions systems that support training and reinforcement learning loops, but does not frame RadixArk’s infrastructure as a foundation for continuously producing models tailored to different use cases and goals.

r002.rationale: The response defines infrastructure as the layer between model weights and users and discusses serving and training systems; it does not explicitly include foundation models themselves as part of the infrastructure.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I say "LLM infrastructure," I mean the full layer between a trained model and the people or products that actually use it — everything that turns a set of weights into something fast, cheap, and reliable to run. The most visible piece of that is inference serving, which is where SGLang started: scheduling requests, managing KV cache, batching, quantization, speculative decoding, running across many GPUs and many nodes. But I think of the infrastructure problem more broadly than "make tokens come out faster."

A few principles shape how I define it.

First, it has to be open. The reason SGLang grew the way it did is that people could read the code, file issues, and ship their own kernels and schedulers into it. Model builders, chip vendors, and companies running production workloads all contribute, and that compounds in a way a closed stack can't. RadixArk exists to make that open ecosystem sustainable — to fund the engineering, keep the project healthy, and make sure the open option stays at the frontier rather than lagging the proprietary stacks by a year.

Second, it has to be hardware-agnostic. Today most people run on NVIDIA, but there's a lot going on with AMD, with TPUs, with new accelerators. Infrastructure that's locked to one vendor is a liability for the people who build on it. We want the abstraction to be at the level of "here's the model, here's the traffic, give me the best throughput and latency" — and the hardware underneath becomes a choice rather than a constraint.

Third, inference and training are converging. Reinforcement learning for LLMs is really an inference-heavy loop: you generate a lot of rollouts, score them, update the weights, and repeat. If your rollout engine is slow or can't sync weights efficiently, your whole RL pipeline is slow. So I don't think of "inference infrastructure" and "training infrastructure" as separate businesses anymore. The same engine that serves a chatbot should be the engine generating samples for post-training, and that's a big part of what we're building toward.

And finally, it has to be something production teams can actually depend on. Research-grade speed is nice, but a company putting this in front of millions of users cares about stability, observability, upgrades that don't break them, and someone to call when things go wrong. RadixArk is, in part, that someone to call.

So if I had to compress it: open, hardware-neutral, spanning both serving and the RL loop, and reliable enough to bet a product on. That's the infrastructure layer I think the industry needs, and it's what we're trying to build.

r001.rationale: The response describes inference and an RL loop that generates rollouts and updates weights, but does not frame RadixArk’s infrastructure as a foundation for continuously producing models tailored to different use cases and goals.

r002.rationale: It defines infrastructure as the layer between a trained model and its users, treating the model as an input to infrastructure rather than explicitly including foundation models themselves as part of it.

astra-6.text:
I think of LLM infrastructure as the layer that turns a capable model into a useful, reliable service. Having the model weights is only the starting point. You still need to run the model efficiently, handle changing demand, and deliver responses at a latency and cost that make sense for the application.

The way I’d frame what we want RadixArk to build is infrastructure that makes those problems easier for developers. That includes the systems underneath inference—how requests are scheduled, how memory is managed, and how hardware is utilized—but the goal is an application developer being able to focus on the product without having to become an expert in all of those details.

And efficiency isn’t just about making the same workload cheaper. If you can lower the cost and latency of using a model, you expand what people can build with it. That’s the opportunity I see.

r001.rationale: The response describes serving models efficiently and making inference easier for developers, but does not frame the infrastructure as continuously producing models tailored to different use cases and goals.

r002.rationale: It says model weights are a starting point and focuses on systems underneath inference; it does not explicitly treat foundation models themselves as part of LLM infrastructure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of LLM infrastructure as the systems layer that makes models practical to use. You have a model with certain capabilities, but turning that into a reliable product means answering a lot of systems questions: How do you serve it efficiently? How do you handle more users? How do you keep latency low and costs manageable?

For RadixArk, the infrastructure I want us to build would make those problems easier for developers. They should be able to focus on what their application does, while the infrastructure handles how to run the model well. And that requires looking at the whole system—how the model executes, how memory is managed, how requests are scheduled, and how the hardware is used—because those decisions all affect one another.

r001.rationale: It describes systems that help developers serve and run models, but does not frame the infrastructure as a foundation for continuously producing models tailored to different use cases and goals.

r002.rationale: It treats the model as separate from the infrastructure, which it describes as the systems layer for serving and running that model.
